paragraphs.heading: A column of open water
paragraphs.text: The pelagic zone is the open, free water away from the shore. It can be pictured as an imaginary cylinder, or water column, running from the sea surface to the bottom. The word pelagic comes from an Ancient Greek word for 'open sea'. In all, the zone holds 1.33 billion km³ of water, with a mean depth of 3.68 km and a maximum depth of 11 km.

paragraphs.heading: What changes on the way down
paragraphs.text: Conditions change with depth. Pressure goes up, while temperature and light go down. Salinity, oxygen and micronutrients such as iron all change too. The water column can be split vertically into as many as five layers, and how many there are depends on how deep the water is. Pelagic life becomes scarcer as depth increases.

paragraphs.heading: The lit zone at the top
paragraphs.text: The zone at the surface is lit, and it is the only one with enough light for photosynthesis. Nearly all of the ocean's primary production happens here. About 90% of marine life is concentrated in it, including plankton, floating seaweed, jellyfish, tuna, whales, sharks and dolphins. The whole pelagic ecosystem is based on phytoplankton.

paragraphs.heading: The mesopelagic zone
paragraphs.text: A boundary called the thermocline separates the warmer top zone from the much colder mesopelagic zone. Only a very small trace of sunlight reaches this zone, and the pressure is about 20 - 100 atm. Because sunlight is lacking, many of the organisms here have evolved adaptations, bioluminescence among them. Some mesopelagic creatures rise at night to feed in a zone called the epipelagic. Heterotrophic bacteria are among the more abundant organisms, and they mainly feed on and break down matter falling from the zone above.

paragraphs.heading: Pitch black water
paragraphs.text: One zone takes its name from the Ancient Greek for 'deep'. It is pitch black, with no trace of sunlight apart from the occasional bioluminescent organism, such as an anglerfish. Its temperature and salinity are stable. Most creatures here live on detritus known as "marine snow" that falls from the zones above. Others, like the marine hatchetfish, prey on fellow inhabitants.

paragraphs.heading: The deepest zones
paragraphs.text: Another zone is named from the Ancient Greek for 'bottomless', and the ocean floor is next to it. Very few creatures live in its cold, high pressure and complete darkness; they include several species of squid, the sea pig and the sea spider. Many species at these depths are transparent and eyeless. One more zone is named after the realm of Hades, the Greek underworld. It is the deepest part of all, more than 6,000 m down, and such depths are generally found in trenches. Pressure here can be 1,100 atm, and very few creatures live in it.
